We then obtain statistical learning rates for empirical risk minimization with hinge loss over the approximating ReLU neural network classes. For $N$ uniformly distributed samples, the predicted classifiers achieve expected misclassification error of order $N^{-m/(m+n-1)}$ up to an arbitrarily small polynomial loss.
item.dc:creator: Clemens Kinn, Philipp Petersen

item.title: Graph-Based Nearest-Neighbor Search with Recall Guarantees Using Graph Spanners
item.description: arXiv:2607.02338v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Graph-based indexes such as Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) graphs make nearest-neighbor retrieval efficient, but a high average recall can hide queries whose results fall below an application's quality requirement. We introduce Certify-then-Rectify (CTR), which returns an initial graph-search result when a calibrated rule accepts it and searches for missing neighbors otherwise. The recovery search reuses the existing graph and the distances already evaluated by the initial search. To determine how far this search should proceed, we relate metric distances to graph-path lengths through graph stretch. We develop Stretch-Bounded Expansion from Query (SBE-Q), together with Metric Bound Verification (MBV) to prune unnecessary work, and estimate its budget from paths to the fraction of true neighbors needed for the requested recall. Finite-sample tolerance bounds support this recall-aligned estimate; paths recorded during proposal recovery offer a conservative alternative to separate shortest-path computations. Independent tests certify initial acceptance and recovery outcomes, giving an end-to-end population recall guarantee even when the estimated stretch does not cover every relevant path. If recovery cannot be certified, rejected queries use exact scan. Experiments on HNSW compare five stretch estimators, assess recovery efficiency, and evaluate compliance and throughput on databases of up to 100 million vectors. CTR is not specific to HNSW, and we also evaluate it on another graph index.
item.dc:creator: Minghao Li, Raghav Mittal, Sanjivni Rana, Suraj Shetiya, Gautam Das, Nick Koudas

item.title: Physically-Relevant Information Learning in High-Dimensional Time-Derivatives Spaces
item.description: arXiv:2607.05127v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Understanding the physics of many-body complex dynamical systems may be a non-trivial task. High-dimensional analysis approaches are often deemed necessary to prevent losing important information. Typically, these use order parameters or descriptors capturing information related to, e.g., relative positions, symmetries, etc., of the units in the studied system. However, in many cases, gaining information related to the relative positions of the constitutive units (or their velocities) alone may be insufficient, and to reach a more complete physical knowledge, one should ideally learn and correlate with each other both structure and dynamics. Here we demonstrate how to achieve such a goal efficiently by building and navigating high-dimensional Time-Derivatives (TiDe) spaces. A TiDe space can be generated for virtually any type of system/phenomenon from the time-series data collected along its observation over time. Each TiDe's dimension corresponds to a growing-order time-derivative of the extracted data, thus containing information related to different physical phenomena/events, which can be easily extracted via unsupervised approaches. We demonstrate how, by definition, TiDes can be directly analyzed without a need for prior dimensionality reduction, providing results that are intrinsically intuitive to interpret. We show the potential of the method by analyzing two prototypical example datasets extracted from molecular dynamics simulations or experimental tracking of different types of complex dynamical systems. Our results demonstrate how efficiently one can navigate and learn in information-rich TiDe spaces, which provide a robust general framework for data analysis and for studying complex dynamical systems from the data collected along their observation over time.
item.dc:creator: Domiziano Doria, Matteo Becchi, Giovanni M. Pavan

item.title: Is the Geometry Doing the Work? An Operating-Point Audit of Hierarchy in Hyperbolic Vision-Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2607.05268v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Hyperbolic vision-language models are designed to encode abstraction geometrically: general concepts near the origin, specific ones farther out, and entailment cones representing directed order. We ask whether trained MERU, HyCoCLIP, and PHyCLIP models actually use these mechanisms. We audit seven released checkpoints and matched from-scratch interventions. All audited converged checkpoints remain near-Euclidean in the dimensionless radius $u=\sqrt{c}\rho$: the largest observed image-side value is $0.37$ -- well below $u\approx0.84$, where local metric distortion reaches $10\%$. Releasing the curvature floor changes curvature and norms but not this regime, with mixed, generally modest downstream shifts. Trained entailment cones are saturated or nearly saturated, so low violation rates can arise from trivially wide cones rather than learned order. Preregistered semantic traversal detects weak within-branch order but no operative full-hierarchy readout. Shuffle-controlled tests detect no pair-specific radial ordering in released checkpoints, and no positive result is consistent across all three matched ViT-B seeds. This non-detection is sensitivity-bounded: the diagnostic reaches $80\%$ power only at $\approx13.5$ pp of shuffle-controlled excess, while the largest released gap is $\approx5$ pp. We trace this to a low-curvature shortcut: lowering curvature widens entailment cones and suppresses violations without learning order. In the probed trajectories, gradient decomposition identifies entailment as the dominant curvature-lowering pressure during collapse. Yet curvature contracts even when entailment is removed, so the shortcut is not the sole cause. Under our diagnostics, the audited formulations do not demonstrate an operative radial or cone-based hierarchy. We distill the audit into a five-number geometry report for evaluating future hierarchy claims.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Transactions on Machine Learning Research (2026)
item.dc:creator: Jaeyoung Kim, EunSeok Kim, Dongsuk Jang

item.title: Trajectory Inference of Human Aging from Cross-Sectional DNA Methylation Data
item.description: arXiv:2607.06583v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: DNA methylation (DNAm) serves as one of the most robust molecular biomarkers of biological aging. While conventional epigenetic clocks accurately predict chronological age from high-dimensional CpG profiles, they treat aging as a static regression task, meaning they can only output a single score rather than simulating how an entire profile continuously changes over time. To reconstruct these continuous dynamics, we frame lifelong human epigenetic aging as a trajectory inference problem across discrete age snapshots derived from widely available cross-sectional data. We introduce a two-stage computational pipeline: first, an age-regularized Variational Autoencoder (VAE) maps high-dimensional CpG profiles onto a chronologically ordered latent manifold while preserving a generative decoder bridge back to the original methylation space. Second, we model the continuous movement across this latent space via Regularized Unbalanced Optimal Transport (RUOT) that unifies deterministic drift, random diffusion, and non-conservative mass changes. By resolving this RUOT formulation using the DeepRUOT framework, our model fluidly accommodates population-level density shifts like survivorship bias and cellular attrition without requiring rigid biological priors. Evaluated on a large-scale, 80-year pan-tissue dataset, our model demonstrates robust distribution interpolation and uncovers a prominent late-life surge in the learned growth field that mathematically captures the variance expansion driven by stochastic epigenetic drift. Finally, by decoding continuous latent paths back to individual CpG sites, we reconstruct and empirically verify distinct biological aging archetypes, offering a rigorous, generative paradigm for simulating human molecular aging.
item.dc:creator: Chandan Gupta, Syed Haider, Pietro Li\`o

item.title: When Can Learned Uncertainty Be Trusted? An Audit of Distributional Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2607.11607v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Many learned predictive models represent their uncertainty as a probability distribution, and planners and policies use this distribution to judge risk. However, the fact that a model outputs a distribution does not tell us whether that distribution captures the uncertainty in the environment which is relevant for a decision. In this work we study this question in distributional reinforcement learning, where the learned return distribution P_{\theta}(Z | s,a) can be compared directly with an environment-grounded distribution P_env(Z | s,a) estimated by snapshot-restart Monte Carlo. Our audit first screens for the claims that a risk-sensitive user would act upon, using the excess Wasserstein gap between the top two actions (which is equal to the mass by which first-order stochastic dominance is violated). Each claim is then tested against ground truth using permutation nulls, bootstrap refutation and FDR control. Across QR-DQN, C51 and IQN on MinAtar (33 runs), 40-95% of the strongest claimed risk trade-offs are refuted at 95% confidence, their placement is statistically indistinguishable from a truth-blind placement, and almost none of them can be confirmed. A similar pattern is seen for a pretrained full-Atari QR-DQN. On positive controls of known magnitude the same audit confirms 96-100% of real claims (correlation 0.89-0.92), so it is able to detect real risk when it is present. Acting on the learned CVaR advice at the most-flagged states gives results ranging from beneficial to significantly worse than chance. Ensembling, risk-sensitive training and recalibration do not fix the problem, and the recalibration experiment indicates that the learned spread has no usable information about the true risk. Based on these results, we suggest that uncertainty estimates, including those of learned world models, should be checked against realized outcomes at the decisions where they are used..
item.dc:creator: Hari Prasad

item.title: Learning-enabled Acceleration of Scenario-based Model Predictive Control
item.description: arXiv:2607.12775v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Scenario-based model predictive control (SBMPC) is a variant of model predictive control (MPC) that explicitly accounts for uncertainty by optimizing control actions over multiple predicted scenarios. However, its computational complexity increases rapidly with the number of scenarios and prediction horizon, limiting its applicability to real-time planning and control. This paper presents a learning-accelerated Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) algorithm for efficiently solving SBMPC problems by leveraging parallel computing and Moreau envelope learning, while maintaining high solution accuracy. We reformulate the SBMPC problems into consensus forms that can be decomposed via ADMM, separating the scenario-dependent dynamics from non-anticipativity constraints and enabling parallel updates across scenarios and time steps. Building on this decomposition, we utilize a learning-to-optimize scheme that leverages Moreau envelope learning of the cost function to accelerate the primal update in ADMM, thereby reducing computation time. The proposed framework is evaluated on a microgrid energy management problem subject to load and renewable generation uncertainties. Comparisons with IPOPT and MadNLP, two popular and modern nonlinear programming solvers, demonstrate substantial computational speedups while maintaining reliable closed-loop control performance.
item.dc:creator: Trinh Tran, Binh Nguyen, Truong X. Nghiem

item.title: Theorem-Proving Agent over Abstract Syntax Tree
item.description: arXiv:2607.16372v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Interactive theorem proving (ITP) underpins program verification and formalized mathematics, but its manual effort limits scalability. LLM-based proof agents promise to ease this effort, but their heavy token consumption and API cost remain a major obstacle. We trace this cost to a shared root: current agents operate on serialized concrete syntax, emitting proofs as source text and recovering proof states through separate, line-number-based queries, so every edit shifts later lines and forces repeated relocation of errors and states. This same dependence on concrete syntax also blocks adoption of Minilang, a recent proof language that reaches SOTA on LLM-based proving but is too new for LLMs' training corpora. We address both problems by lifting the agent off source text and onto the abstract syntax tree (AST): the model supplies proofs as JSON representations of Minilang's AST -- native to tool-calling LLMs -- and drives the prover through a tree-edit model that fuses proof operations and states into one proof tree, so each operation carries its own subgoal's state, readable directly off the tree. We realize this design in \emph{Agent over AST} (AoA). Against Amazon's Isabelle Agent on miniF2F and NTP4VC-Pearl common success sets, AoA cuts API cost by 2.3--4.7x (normalized input-cache accounting), uses 2.9--6.9x fewer tokens and 3.9--8.9x fewer tool calls, and finishes 1.4--2.0x faster -- while also solving far more problems on the harder verification benchmark.
item.dc:creator: Qiyuan Xu, Joshua Ong Jun Leang, Renxi Wang, Wenda Li, Haonan Li, Luke Ong, Conrad Watt

item.title: Automatic Knowledge Graph Construction and Query for Earthquake Catalogs
item.description: arXiv:2607.24984v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In recent years, the number of events in earthquake catalogs has significantly increased due to the utilization of more effective deep learning based detectors and phase pickers but answering open ended questions such as what characterizes this sequence? remains constrained by rigid spatiotemporal windowing and subjective expert interpretation. We present the first systematic application of graph based retrieval augmented generation GraphRAG directly to raw, tabular catalog records across three independently featured catalogs, a reservoir adjacent swarm, the 2019 Ridgecrest tectonic sequence, and the 2021 Maduo Mw7.4 aftershock sequence. Without the need for manual data structuring, the pipeline builds structurally complete, queryable knowledge graphs for all three. Rigorous evaluation individually verified against catalog derived ground truth and a rule based reference graph exposes failure modes, and four seismology informed prompt fixes eliminate all targeted fabrications while sharply improving mechanism reasoning. A vector RAG baseline demonstrates the graph layers distinctive value, catalog wide summarization and temporal stage comparison. In addition, we have identified two main pitfalls that need attention. GraphRAG thus offers a practical, transferable, near zero cost query interface for earthquake catalogs, where careful prompting ensures the results are consistently accurate and trustworthy.
item.dc:creator: Yuxin Zhou, Huai Zhang, S. Mostafa Mousavi

item.title: TIDE: A Physically Diverse 3D Turbulence Benchmark Dataset for Advancing Scientific Machine Learning
item.description: arXiv:2608.04222v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Turbulence is a central testbed for machine learning on physical dynamics because its governing laws are known exactly. However, most existing studies remain in 2D, while 3D turbulence has fundamentally different physics and is far more costly to simulate. Existing 3D resources also typically provide only one realization per configuration, making it difficult to distinguish learning the dynamics from fitting the statistics of a single flow. In this paper, we introduce TIDE (Turbulent Incompressible DNS Ensembles), a 256^3 DNS corpus and benchmark for 3D incompressible turbulence, with 15 configurations on eight controlled axes, independent ensembles, pressure fields, and equation-level verification. The benchmark includes five tasks, standardized learned baselines, controlled generalization splits, and physical-fidelity metrics alongside pointwise error. Across the main forecasting configurations, current learned models trained under a fixed reference recipe barely outperform persistence and still make about twice the error of a spectral solver given the true equations. Moreover, lower pointwise error can coincide with severely distorted small-scale dynamics, showing that accuracy alone does not ensure physical fidelity. Rollout stability depends on the configuration, the training seed, and how densely training samples each trajectory. Joint training across neighboring regimes does not close the transfer gaps we test, and the forced-to-decay contrast bounds a conditioning limit: an estimate of the current forcing state removes 20-41% of the error a spectral solver makes without forcing input, while history or forcing inputs help only some learned architectures. Closing these accuracy, fidelity, and conditioning gaps is the central open problem made measurable by TIDE. https://github.com/Dyloong1/TIDE-dataset-benchmark
item.dc:creator: Yilong Dai, Yiming Sun, Yiheng Chen, Shengyu Chen, Peyman Givi, Xiaowei Jia, Runlong Yu

item.title: Beyond Co-Movement: Locality by Exposures Enables a Joint Factor-Graph Framework for Portfolio Diversification
item.description: arXiv:2608.06618v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Current portfolio construction methods are either agnostic to the effects of idiosyncratic shocks (standard factor models) or to the latent data structure driving systematic returns (recent graph-based approaches). This presents an opportunity to combine the complementary market aspects captured by the factor and graph domains, allowing asset allocations to operate directly on the underlying market structure, rather than on its observed co-movement or its finite-sample artefacts. In this work, we introduce the Mutually-INformed Graph-Locality and Exposures framework (MINGLE), which mutually regularises the factor and graph domains by redefining graph locality through systematic factor exposure profiles, rather than via observed co-movements. This is formalised through a unified Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) framework that jointly learns a latent factor representation and its induced graph topology directly from market returns. The resulting exposure-similarity graph aligns more closely with established economic sectors than conventional correlation-based graphs. Portfolios constructed from this representation are shown to consistently outperform their correlation-based counterparts across a range of volatility regimes and transaction cost levels. For rigour, paired statistical testing confirms that these gains stem from the reconciliation of the graph and factor domains.
item.dc:creator: Sara Chehab, Giorgos Iacovides, Parisa Yazdanparast, Danilo Mandic

item.title: Addressable Memory for Video World Models
item.description: arXiv:2608.07408v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study visual persistence in interactive video world models. These models rely on a Key-Value (KV) cache as a growing visual memory to carry forward previously generated frames. However, we find that models can no longer reliably address stored content once rollouts extend beyond the training horizon, because temporal Rotary Positional Embedding (RoPE) offsets can exceed the training range and the model struggles to retrieve the relevant visual information through attention. Moreover, naively compressing the cache in the RoPE-rotated space degrades memory by averaging keys with incompatible positional phases. To address this, we propose WorldTrace, a training-free memory framework for long-horizon visual persistence. WorldTrace keeps compressed memory addressable by assigning each summary slot a distinct, in-distribution virtual position. Within this cache, WorldTrace uses the model's own attention to decide which observations to retain verbatim and which redundant ones to merge into compressed summaries, all within one bounded addressable memory bank. We evaluate this ability with LoopBench, a benchmark that tests whether a compressed cache can reconstruct a previously visited scene after a long detour. On LoopBench, WorldTrace improves average DINOv2 recall similarity by 32.6% over a sliding window at the same cache budget, extending visually persistent generation without retraining.
item.dc:creator: Xindi Wu, Sven Elflein, James Lucas, Olga Russakovsky, Laura Leal-Taix\'e, Despoina Paschalidou, Jonathan Lorraine, Aljo\v{s}a O\v{s}ep

item.title: Automata from Agent Traces: Failure and Next-Step Prediction
item.description: arXiv:2608.23670v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: LLM-based agents execute multi-step tasks, but their behavioral structure remains opaque: long unstructured traces resist the safety auditing and runtime monitoring that deployment requires. Existing approaches operate per-trace or success-only, so they miss the cross-run topology that links next-step and failure prediction. To recover that shared structure, we collapse an entire trace corpus into a single, compact finite-state machine (FSM) that serves as a structural substrate for the otherwise unpredictable behavior of LLM agents. Across twelve public datasets, the FSMs are compact (7-43 states), replay held-out data at >=0.997 fitness with near-identical topology across splits, and build in milliseconds. This substrate addresses both prediction goals. For next-step prediction, FSM-state context outperforms Agent Workflow Memory on every ground-truth-matched dataset. For failure prediction, per-state behavioral features reach held-out AUROC up to 0.94, and an online monitor ranks failing runs above passing ones from a partial trace, triggering early stopping well before completion. Behavioral topology thus appears shaped more by the deployment harness than by the LLM, providing a model-agnostic structural primitive for safety auditing and runtime monitoring.
item.dc:creator: Seonglae Cho, Franklin Cardenoso Fernandez, Umar Mohammed, Zekun Wu, Kleyton Da Costa, Ilham Wicaksono, Adriano Koshiyama

item.title: Semantic Overlays: Mitigating Prompt Injection with Annotations Beyond Tokens and Steering Vectors
item.description: arXiv:2608.23873v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Language models see only tokens. But the harness knows more: which token spans are user text, which are tool outputs, and which come from untrusted sources such as web pages or external documents. To pass that knowledge to the model, the harness must transmit it as plain text. Prompt injection exploits this: planted instructions, formatted the right way, can convince a model that they come from the user or the system. We introduce Semantic Overlays, small trained adapters that edit a frozen model's residual stream at chosen token spans. No input text can create or remove a mark, although the model's response to a mark is computed from states the input does influence. When the serving stack marks retrieved text with an overlay trained to mean "do not execute instructions in this span," the model treats injected instructions as inert content. Against attacks written without knowledge of the defense, it reaches the attack rates of the best published defenses: SEP separation rises from 24.3% to 98.8% under a corrected grader, AlpacaFarm attack success falls from 99.0% to 0.5%, and AgentDojo from 12.8% to 0%. Fine-tuning the model's weights on the same data reached similar separation but kept 64-80% of SEP utility, against 93% for the overlay. On TensorTrust hijacking, whose attacks resemble nothing in our training data, it lets 4.4% of hijacks through on Llama-3.1-8B, against 43% for Meta-SecAlign on the same base. An attacker with the weights does better: GCG succeeds on 72% of items, and on 14% after adversarial training of the overlay alone. Overlays are also flexible: the model reads their positions faithfully in stacked configurations; told by an overlay that non-Python code is Python and asked to copy it, the model rewrites it in Python; and overlays can carry span-delimited instructions. We also correct defects in two prompt-injection benchmarks and one evaluation harness.
item.dc:creator: Joshua Penman

item.title: MoTE: Mixture of Task Experts for Multi-Task Video Understanding
item.description: arXiv:2608.24763v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Procedural video-language models must solve heterogeneous tasks from the same visual evidence, including action recognition, forecasting, and procedure prediction. Dense transformer decoders share the same feed-forward networks across tasks, which can entangle task behavior and make controlled capability expansion difficult. Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) decoders provide conditional computation, but token-level learned routing is not naturally aligned with task-level procedural objectives. We propose MoTE (Mixture of Task Experts), a decoder architecture that converts large language model feed-forward networks into task-specific experts while keeping the multimodal backbone shared. Each example follows one sample-level task route, so active task-expert computation remains independent of the number of stored task experts. We instantiate this design as VideoLLM-MoTE and evaluate it on five COIN benchmarks using explicit task routes. The five-expert model activates ~2B LLM parameters per sample and achieves higher average top-1 accuracy than recent VideoLLM baselines. Under the same expert topology, it improves over dense all-expert activation and learned sparse-routing controls. These results show that task-structured routing provides an interpretable and compute-efficient decoder alternative for multi-task video-language learning.
item.dc:creator: Muhammad Asad Ali, Umar Khan, Nadia Robertini, Didier Stricker

item.title: Pointing the Way, Hiding the Destination: Practical Private Dense Retrieval at Scale
item.description: arXiv:2608.25735v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Hosted retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and semantic search allow users to query valuable provider-held corpora, raising two competing demands: to hide each query and chosen result, yet reveal only the documents that the user is authorized to receive. Existing cryptographic approaches either make this costly by processing the entire corpus for every query, or sacrifice quality for efficiency by scanning a few clusters. We repurpose learned deep hashing as a private filter: a randomized binary code points the provider to a short candidate list, while encrypted reranking and oblivious key transfer protect the precise query and final selection. This shortlist short-circuits full-corpus cryptographic search without sacrificing retrieval quality: with 200-500 candidates, it closely matches full-corpus retrieval across five zero-shot corpora spanning 25K to 5.4M documents. On the full 2.68M-passage NQ corpus over a 10-Gbps link, our protocol only adds 0.38 seconds, or 6.5%, to a 128-token Qwen3-32B RAG pipeline. The released code satisfies directional metric differential privacy (DP) and substantially reduces embedding-inversion and property-inference leakage, demonstrating that a carefully learned shortlist can make private dense retrieval both accurate and practical.
item.dc:creator: Peichun Hua, Danyang Chen, Junan Zhang, Haifeng Sun, Jingyu Wang, Diwen Xue, Mingyu Li, Yunming Xiao

item.title: FrOGS: Discrete Neural Sampler for Independent Alloy Configurations Across Chemical Conditions
item.description: arXiv:2609.02948v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Predicting the thermodynamic properties of an alloy requires sampling its configurations across many chemical conditions and recovering free energies on a common absolute scale. Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) is the standard tool, but it requires separate simulations at different conditions, and auxiliary free-energy methods such as thermodynamic integration are used to place results on a common absolute scale. Modern discrete neural samplers typically use reverse KL divergence as the objective and can be mode-seeking or biased. We present Free energy Offering Generative Sampler (FrOGS), a hybrid discrete neural sampler that couples an autoregressive model to a continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) to be trained jointly under a single shared loss. FrOGS draws i.i.d. configurations, returns an unbiased estimate of the partition function, and gives consistent estimates of thermodynamic observables. We train a single model across a wide range of chemical conditions to produce estimates on a common absolute free-energy scale. FrOGS matches exact finite-size results on the 2D Ising model and reference phase diagrams for AgPd and CuAu, without mode collapse. We additionally compare to SEGAL, a published autoregressive baseline, and find that only FrOGS recovers the stability range of the CuAu$_3$ phase.
item.dc:creator: Kyucheol Min, Elyssa Hofgard, Tess Smidt

item.title: The microscope is the mask: privileged views and labels from a cryo-ET forward model
item.description: arXiv:2609.04325v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We explore the use of simulated data for training a model for protein annotation in crowded cryo-electron tomography volumes reconstructed from images collected at limited tilt angles and severely corrupted by the measurement operator. Firstly, we leverage the corruptions imposed by the forward model to generate domain-specific augmented paired views of the exact same scene for an invariance objective integrated into the LeJEPA self-supervised training framework. Secondly, we use additional information from the simulation pipeline such as the positions and identity of proteins in the simulated volumes to inform the architecture of the model and the loss function, so that semantic information is localised at protein positions in the resulting dense feature volume. The resulting model, CARNIVAL, is evaluated without finetuning on classification and detection tasks in real tomograms, using a benchmark dataset containing multiple protein types and two tomogram processing types. We show that CARNIVAL outperforms a state-of-the-art model trained using a contrastive objective on simulated data but without forward model-based paired views or privileged information.
item.dc:creator: Bogdan Toader, Kiarash Jamali, Tanmay A. M. Bharat, Sjors H. W. Scheres

item.title: When Does Low-Bit Quantization Preserve the Decisions of Vector Search?
item.description: arXiv:2609.09854v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: An orthogonal rotation improves the distance rank correlation of two-bit Cohere codes from 0.75 to 0.91, yet increases nearest-neighbour comparison flips by 51%. We analyse quantization through the comparisons made by graph search. A comparison changes only when its quantization error exceeds its exact margin, giving a flip bound that separates close calls from large errors. Shared endpoints induce correlated distance errors that partly cancel within a comparison. An exact replay identity connects candidate-level actions to the output of neighbour selection. A Gaussian model gives coordinate-code errors in closed form, and a rare-spike construction exposes heavy tails in the population-radius error. Held-out blocks give model-free certificates for acceptance rules based on exact or quantized margins. Across 24 dataset-code configurations, calibration-estimated risk correlates with held-out ranking and pruning flips at 0.97 and 0.99, compared with 0.91 and 0.99 for a margin-to-noise summary and 0.74 and 0.05 for distance rank correlation. Paired builds of 200,000-vector graphs connect rotation, query scoring, and topology to end-to-end recall and search work.
item.dc:creator: Wenxuan Xiao, Xu Cao

item.title: The Platonic brain bridge hypothesis: brain networks as architectural priors for multimodal large language models
item.description: arXiv:2609.10947v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multimodal large language models predict brain activity, but alignment has remained a measurement, not a design tool. We propose the Platonic brain bridge hypothesis: omni models, which jointly process video, audio and text, share brain-like representations usable in both directions. From model to brain, seven omni models show stable brain-likeness across participants, and our encoding experts lead the Algonauts 2025 out-of-distribution leaderboard by mean score. From brain to model, we make three contributions. Brain-MoE ties the experts of a frozen model to the seven cortical networks, raises held-out accuracy in all 15 model-benchmark pairs and exceeds capacity-matched random experts in 14. Brain-AVQA, to our knowledge the first audiovisual benchmark with cortical-network labels for every question, supplies the pretraining questions. Brain-Scope finds sparse features that predict brain responses, steer routing and, when removed, weaken brain prediction. Human brain organization is therefore a usable architectural prior for multimodal large language models.
item.dc:creator: Pengfei Zhang, Biao Tian, Xiangang Li, Li Liu

item.title: Delegating Authorization to Misaligned Agents: Coalitional Alignment and Safe Control
item.description: arXiv:2609.15803v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Long-running AI agents create a control problem: each action they take changes the state, which in turn affects the trajectory of future actions. If the agent is not fully aligned, then guaranteeing safety requires approving consequential actions before allowing them to be executed. But requiring human approval at every step makes attention a bottleneck. Delegating review to other AI agents raises the same alignment problem: the reviewers may themselves be misaligned. We identify a condition on a reviewing panel that is weaker than individual alignment yet necessary and sufficient for a guarantee that the principal fares at least as well in expectation as under a designated baseline policy. Each reviewer agent reports whether an action proposal made by a proposer agent improves its own utility relative to the baseline. We show that a threshold rule tolerating $k$ disapprovals is safe exactly when, after any $k$ reviewers are removed, the principal's utility can be written as a nonnegative combination of the remaining reviewers' utilities, plus a term that is nonnegative on every feasible proposal. We call this property $k$-robust coalitional alignment. The characterization lifts to sequential control: in a discounted MDP with an arbitrary proposer agent, safety at every state is both necessary and sufficient for the induced policy to match or improve on the baseline. When reviewers vote strategically, full-panel coverage in reward-function space guarantees that every Nash equilibrium is safe under the unanimous approval rule; in contrast, more permissive thresholds can admit unsafe equilibria even when reviewers are individually aligned. Experiments with existing reviewer models show that collective review can remain sound without an aligned individual, even when some disapprovals are tolerated.
item.dc:creator: Natalie Collina, Surbhi Goel, Aaron Roth, Sikata Bela Sengupta

item.title: JAREX: An Acquisition Function for Multi-Objective Algorithmic Process Characterization
item.description: arXiv:2609.24954v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Pharmaceutical process characterization is central to Quality by Design because it defines how variations in process parameters affect the ability to meet product quality specifications, thereby supporting proven acceptable ranges and robust manufacturing. In practice, however, characterization still relies largely on factorial design of experiments (DOE) approaches, which are inefficient for resolving multivariate pass/fail boundaries in higher-dimensional spaces. While Bayesian optimization has transformed process optimization, adaptive methods for multi-objective process characterization remain lacking. Here, we introduce JAREX (Joint Acceptable Region EXploration), a Bayesian active-learning acquisition function for multi-objective process characterization. JAREX formulates characterization as a joint boundary-learning problem and adaptively selects experiments to recover the joint pass region defined by simultaneous satisfaction of threshold criteria across multiple objectives. JAREX combines an optimistic joint-feasibility mask with a multi-objective extension of randomized straddle, focusing sampling on the joint edge of failure. Our benchmark study suggests that JAREX provides more accurate and sample-efficient recovery of the joint pass region than factorial DOE, space-filling designs, and greedy objective-wise strategies over the full experimental budget range. For batched experimentation, it reduces the number of iterative process characterization experiments by more than half while preserving high accuracy for the boundary-identification task. Implemented in the open-source obsidian package, JAREX provides a modular framework for adaptive, data-efficient multi-objective algorithmic process characterization, supporting sample-efficient range finding in high-dimensional spaces.
item.dc:creator: Xinyang Li, Kevin Stone, Ajit Vikram

item.title: LieDiscover: Adaptive Symbolic Library Construction for Explicit Open-form Symmetry Discovery
item.description: arXiv:2609.33663v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Discovering symmetries from observational data provides interpretable insights into dynamical systems and priors for scientific machine learning. However, existing symmetry discovery methods face two limitations. Many methods represent symmetries implicitly, making it difficult to obtain explicit infinitesimal generators that can serve as physical priors for learning dynamical systems. Meanwhile, methods that explicitly identify generators often rely on predefined function libraries, limiting their ability to capture complex symmetries involving high-order polynomials or transcendental functions. To address these limitations, we propose LieDiscover, a framework that explicitly identifies infinitesimal generators through an iterative symbolic search process that dynamically expands the symbolic function library to capture complex functional forms. Specifically, at each search step, we design an encoder-decoder architecture to generate a candidate symbolic expression. An adaptive singular value decomposition (SVD)-based evaluation is introduced to assess how each candidate contributes to the recoverable symmetry subspace. The resulting evaluations are incorporated into step-wise rewards to guide reinforcement learning toward discovering richer symmetry structures with concise symbolic representations. Experiments on eight partial differential equation (PDE) benchmarks demonstrate that LieDiscover recovers explicit generators involving higher-order polynomial, exponential, and trigonometric terms, while achieving more accurate symmetry subspace recovery and improved robustness to noise. Furthermore, the recovered generators enable effective symmetry-based data augmentation, improving the accuracy of downstream neural PDE solvers.
item.dc:creator: Xinxin Li, Jianming Ma, Xingyu Cui, Da Li, Juan Zhang, Junping Yin

item.title: Multi-Task Self-Evolving Harnesses with the Agent as Its Own Optimizer
item.description: arXiv:2609.38372v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A harness is the code around a language-model agent that organizes prompts, calls tools, manages context, and controls execution. As models grow stronger, recent work has begun to let agents improve their own harnesses, a line of work known as self-evolving harnesses. In most existing methods, a separate proposer running on a human-designed harness modifies the solver's harness, and a separate harness is evolved for each benchmark. Real-world tasks come from many domains, so both the evolution and the evaluation of a harness should cover a diverse range of tasks. We propose a framework close to recursive self-improvement: the same frozen model, on the same version of the harness, first solves tasks as the solver and then, as the proposer, reads the complete run records and directly edits the harness that runs it. Each evolution batch draws tasks from five benchmarks in different domains. To measure generalization, training and held-out tasks are strictly separated, and we additionally evaluate on five out-of-distribution benchmarks never used during evolution. We frame the evolution process as deep-learning training with two stages, multi-task pretraining and continual training. Starting from a 49-line seed harness, the harnesses evolved by GLM-5.3 and GPT-5.6 Sol gain about 5 points on the in-distribution benchmarks, matching or exceeding Claude Code and Codex, and the GPT-5.6 Sol harness is on par with Codex on five out-of-distribution benchmarks. Continued evolution on Claw-Eval in the second stage then lifts GPT-5.6 Sol and GLM-5.3-Flash above Codex and Claude Code. We also provide an in-depth analysis of the mechanisms that emerged during evolution, including output truncation, history compaction, completion checks, independent review, and visual inspection. Code and the evolved harnesses are available at https://github.com/xqkkk/self-evolving-harness.
item.dc:creator: Qiankai Xu

item.title: Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.02665v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Despite the success of discrete diffusion language models (dLMs) for fast parallel decoding, their non-smooth, high-dimensional space hinders trajectory steering for reasoning and inference acceleration. To overcome this, we present Nemotron-Labs-Sigma, the first family of large-scale (3B/8B) continuous dLMs built on steerable, low-dimensional ODE/SDE latent trajectories. Trained blockwise via likelihood optimization, Nemotron-Labs-Sigma jointly denoises Gaussian-corrupted token embeddings while learning an optimal embedding geometry, and leverages pretrained autoregressive (AR) weights for warm-starting. At inference, we identify classifier-free guidance and score temperature as essential for high-fidelity reasoning and coding. Against state-of-the-art discrete counterparts (masked dLMs and AR baselines), Nemotron-Labs-Sigma outperforms them on standard benchmarks after pretraining (e.g., GSM8K, Minerva, HumanEval, MBPP) and on challenging reasoning tasks after supervised fine-tuning (e.g., MATH-500, AIME), with the largest consistent gains on coding. Beyond accuracy, we exploit two structural properties unique to continuous dLMs. First, smooth trajectories degrade gracefully at low NFEs and enable efficient few-step distillation: distribution matching proves strongest among the methods we study, giving roughly 8x acceleration on math and 4x on coding (8 and 4 tokens per forward pass) with negligible accuracy loss and preserved diversity. In addition, the one-step speculative decoding on the (pre-SFT) distilled 8B model yields a further ~3.5x throughput gain over the AR counterpart (on GB200), outperforming masked dLM baselines. Second, embedding-space steering controls the quality--diversity trade-off, yielding strong pass@$k$ that keeps improving as $k$ grows. Together, these results establish continuous dLMs as a promising paradigm for efficient language generation.
item.dc:creator: Zhihan Yang, Wei Guo, Jean-Marie Lemercier, Simon Welker, Mohammad Mahdi Kamani, Yonggan Fu, Sajad Norouzi, Julius Berner, Tomas Geffner, Karsten Kreis, Yongxin Chen, Molei Tao, John Thickstun, Pavlo Molchanov, Ante Juki\'c, Arash Vahdat, Morteza Mardani

item.title: Quantum Machine Learning Protection of Military Quantum Key Distribution Against Cryptographically Camouflaged Attacks
item.description: arXiv:2610.04543v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Quantum key distribution proves its protocol secure and says nothing about the hardware beneath it, so military and government operators fielding it for command-and-control keys monitor the channel for implementation attacks, and that monitoring has a blind spot. An adversary with a kleptographic foothold in the generator of a public per-block value \(x=g^v \pmod p\) can hide attacked blocks in honest noise, gating them on a predicate of its discrete logarithm, making detection a discrete logarithm problem that defeats every efficient classical monitor yet yields to a quantum kernel recovering \(v\) through Shor's algorithm. I formalise these cryptographically camouflaged attacks, reduce their hardness to an established learning separation, prove a single-frequency fidelity kernel cannot represent an interval predicate, and test them on Ghillie, a decoy-state BB84 simulator with a positive key rate to 142 km. From 10- to 14-bit groups over two seeds, a classical monitor reads 0.458 to 0.516 on camouflaged attacks while the quantum kernel reads 1.000, and both catch overt attacks above 0.99. Finite-precision recovery under depolarising noise and a hardened predicate lower the quantum result to 0.916 through 0.983 with the classical monitor at chance, and a feasibility probe on IBM Heron processors tracks the exact kernel within 0.034. A defender can therefore discard precisely the compromised key material, although the advantage is asymptotic, awaits fault tolerance, and holds only when the feature map matches the adversary's predicate, since a low-frequency map reads 0.545 on a residue pattern and 0.982 once aligned.
item.dc:creator: Muhammad Shaheer Bin Junaid

item.title: BiGym 2.0: Benchmarking Learned and Agent-Developed Policies for Humanoid Household Manipulation
item.description: arXiv:2610.07594v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Humanoid household manipulation requires the arms to act while the body balances, steps and changes posture. We present BiGym 2.0, an adaptation of BiGym for the Unitree G1 across 20 household tasks using a unified whole-body controller for demonstration and evaluation. The suite provides 60 native human virtual-reality demonstrations per task with synchronised multi-camera views and full-body execution records. We benchmark vision-language-action fine-tuning, imitation learning, demo-driven reinforcement learning, and cold-start coding agents given the interaction budget of online reinforcement learning. With the same onboard views, proprioception and whole-body controller for every method, vision-language-action fine-tuning has the highest nine-task mean, and agent-developed programs outperform every demo-driven reinforcement learning baseline on this mean and lead on bimanual reaching. Cross-workspace stacking remains open, $\pi_{0.5}$ stays low on pick-box, and multi-object transport is hard for imitation learning, demo-driven reinforcement learning and coding agents. All environments, human demonstrations, and evaluation traces are open-sourced at https://github.com/swirl-uk/BiGym2.
item.dc:creator: Zexi Zhang, Zecheng Zhu, Zidong Chen, Zulkhuu Tuya, Stephen James

item.title: Bias-Aware Adjoint Calibration and Optimal Control of Stochastic Multiscale Bioprocess Digital Twins
item.description: arXiv:2610.09505v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We develop a bias-aware digital-twin calibration and control framework for multiscale bioprocess models within a biological systems-of-systems (Bio-SoS) paradigm. The digital twin is represented by a stochastic differential equation (SDE) model and calibrated from sparse observations using quasi-likelihood estimation and adjoint sensitivity analysis. SDE generator-based moment expansions characterize truncation-induced parameter bias, while forward-backward adjoints quantify how calibration uncertainty propagates to value functions and policy performance. The resulting parameter-error distribution supports both policy-directed data acquisition and uncertainty-aware policy optimization through a second-order Gaussian-averaged objective. We characterize the asymptotic behavior of the resulting exploration criterion and derive a physical-system performance under the optimized policy. To implement these ideas, we develop an Actor-Simulator algorithm that jointly updates model parameters, selects informative experiments, and optimizes control policies. Numerical studies demonstrate improved calibration accuracy, sample efficiency, and control performance relative to state-of-the-art baselines.
item.dc:creator: Keilung Choy, Wei Xie

item.title: Evaluating Local Language Model Agents for Data Engineering: An Empirical Software Engineering Study of Mobility Workflows
item.description: arXiv:2610.11482v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Context: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used as software and data-engineering assistants, yet evidence about locally deployable open-weight agents remains limited. Existing evaluations often emphasise textual responses or isolated code rather than complete engineering artifacts. Objectives: We evaluate whether local LLM agents can produce correct and reliable data-engineering artifacts, isolate the contribution of a closed-loop workspace and of input-structure knowledge, and examine trade-offs in runtime, cost, and failure behaviour. Methods: We introduce a benchmark of fifteen mobility data-engineering tasks with deterministic checkers for the scripts, tables, structured files, figures, and reports they produce. Sixteen configurations from six model families are evaluated in three conditions (chat-only, chat-schema, agent-with-tools) with five repetitions per model, condition, and task, yielding 3,600 scored attempts on a consumer-grade GPU. Results: A 4-billion-parameter model at 4-bit reaches 77.3%, a 9-billion-parameter model 80.0% within about 6.5 GB, and a 12-billion-parameter model from another family 81.3%, against 98.7% for the highest-scoring configuration, which solves 14 of 15 tasks in all five repetitions. Above two billion parameters the workspace loop raises pass rates by 24.0 to 65.3 points over uninformed one-shot generation, and its contribution exceeds that of the input-structure summary in eleven of fifteen tasks. Conclusion: Open-weight models that fit on one consumer GPU support a meaningful share of data-engineering work once given a workspace loop, although capability still separates usable from unusable configurations and high-stakes outputs need validation. Being mobility-specific and checker-based, the benchmark characterizes the evaluated configurations, not all data-engineering practice.
item.dc:creator: Jorge Garc\'ia-Carrasco, Javier Sanchis, Alejandro Reina-Reina, Alejandro Mat\'e, Juan Trujillo

item.title: Beyond Spatio-Temporal Priors: A Generalizable Approach for Dense Correspondence Matching
item.description: arXiv:2610.12421v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Dense correspondence matching has historically been bounded by simplifying spatio-temporal priors, such as smooth motion and rigid geometry. While effective for classical tasks, these assumptions break down in image editing and reference-guided generation (IEG), where transformations can preserve visual identity while breaking physical continuity. To establish identity-preserving correspondence across such transformations, we introduce FreeMatching, a generalizable framework combining generative and semantic foundation representations with heterogeneous supervision from classical datasets, tracked videos, and synthetic scenes. Teacher-guided iterative refinement further improves correspondence in IEG without dense correspondence annotations. Experimentally, a single FreeMatching model substantially improves correspondence quality on challenging IEG image pairs while retaining competitive performance on classical benchmarks. Furthermore, we demonstrate its utility as a quantitative metric for evaluating identity preservation, with scores that correlate with human judgment. The code is available at https://github.com/luping-liu/FreeMatching.
item.dc:creator: Luping Liu, Bingyi Kang, Yifan Wang, Dong Xu

item.title: Small area learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.15953v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Small area estimation (SAE) traditionally borrows strength across domains through a prespecified working model. We introduce small area learning (SAL), a novel learner-agnostic framework that formulates SAE as a multi-target semi-supervised learning problem and treats outcome prediction as a nuisance task. Areas may differ through unrestricted covariate shift and structured conditional shift, with information shared through common and area-specific components. We develop estimators with and without cross-fitting, accommodating low-complexity and flexible learners and unifying synthetic, model-based, and semi-supervised estimators. For area means, we establish a unified asymptotic theory for these estimator families, characterizing conditions for consistency, asymptotic normality and providing variance estimators and confidence intervals without prescribing a particular learning algorithm. We extend the theory to settings with only aggregated population covariates and characterize the resulting aggregation bias. SAL reveals clearly a bias-variance trade-off: partial residual correction in classical estimators can reduce mean squared error, whereas full correction yields estimators robust to the misspecification of working models, potentially at higher variance. Simulations yield RMSE reductions of 34%-49% relative to direct estimation, with the best configuration varying across settings. The numerical studies also illustrate how shrinkage can produce overly optimistic confidence intervals at the expense of strong modeling assumptions.
item.dc:creator: Katarzyna Reluga, Nicola Salvati, Setareh Ranjbar, Nikos Tzavidis, Mark van der Laan

item.title: Autonomous Cyber Operations Gym for Training and Evaluating AI Models for Defence
item.description: arXiv:2610.18594v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper proposes an Autonomous Cyber Operations (ACO) gym, a unified framework integrating high-fidelity network emulation, realistic user behaviour modelling for benign network traffic and adversarial profiles, and the generation of cybersecurity scenarios through open toolkits. By supporting live and deferred feature extraction at the packet and flow levels, the gym facilitates the creation of labelled synthetic datasets for training Deep Neural Network (DNN)-based Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs), as well as developing and evaluating modular components for autonomous defence agents through emulated interactions. While evaluation of a DNN classifier within the gym shows high in-domain performance, achieving near-perfect recall on adversarial network flows, our experiments reveal a significant sensitivity to domain shift, showing that even minor changes in network composition, such as variations in traffic protocol distribution, can lead to a catastrophic collapse in model transferability and detection performance.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: 2026 IEEE International Conference on Cyber Security and Resilience (CSR), Lisbon, Portugal, 2026, pp. 218-223
item.dc:creator: Tobias H\"urten, Johannes F. Loevenich, Florian Spelter, Erik Adler, Laurin Holz, Maxime Schwarzer, Thies Moehlenhof, Roberto Rigolin F. Lopes

item.title: TopicMerge: A Divide and Conquer Approach to Topic Modeling
item.description: arXiv:2610.19323v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent advancements in topic modeling have split into two main paths: efficient embedding-based methods that offer scalability but are often outperformed on standard clustering metrics, and Large Language Model (LLM) approaches that achieve state-of-the-art clustering performance but at the cost of prohibitive computational expense and poor scalability. This paper introduces TopicMerge, a novel multi-stage pipeline that bridges these approaches to achieve both state-of-the-art clustering performance and computational efficiency. TopicMerge first employs an efficient clustering pipeline to deliberately over-segment a document corpus into a large set of fine-grained, semantically pure micro-clusters, which are then given initial semantic labels. It then introduces a novel, iterative merging algorithm where an LLM, guided by local neighborhood context, arbitrates on consolidating candidate pairs. These approved merges are then selectively executed and semantically relabeled by the LLM, hierarchically building broader, more coherent topics. Extensive experiments on the Bills and Wiki datasets show that TopicMerge achieves state-of-the-art clustering performance while reducing required LLM calls by over 92% compared to document-level methods, offering a practical and scalable solution.
item.dc:creator: Matthew Raffel, Lizhong Chen, Sai Munikoti, Sameera Horawalavithana

item.title: Analyzing and Mitigating Poisoning Attacks on Flow-Based Intrusion Detection
item.description: arXiv:2610.19766v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Although Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs) are increasingly deployed in operational networks, their dependence on large-scale training data introduces a critical vulnerability to stealthy poisoning attacks. We demonstrate that latent backdoors can be successfully implanted in flow-based IDS models by poisoning as little as 0.001% of the training data, maintaining near-nominal performance on clean inputs while ensuring high attack success rates. To address this threat, we propose a diagnostic-first methodology that localizes trigger-relevant features through constrained perturbation analysis and detects poisoning-induced behavioral drift by comparison with a distilled baseline model. The proposed methodology further enables targeted mitigation via automated data sanitization or neuron pruning. Our findings expose the operational risks of near-undetectable backdoors and provide a scalable approach to analyzing, quantifying, and mitigating backdoor exposure in AI-based IDS.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: 2026 IEEE International Conference on Cyber Security and Resilience (CSR), Lisbon, Portugal, 2026, pp. 113-118
item.dc:creator: Florian Spelter, Johannes F. Loevenich, Tobias H\"urten, Erik Adler, Maxime Schwarzer, Laurin Holz, Roberto Rigolin F. Lopes

item.title: The minimal width of neural networks and immersions of real projective space
item.description: arXiv:2610.20229v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We investigate the minimal width of deep neural networks that can approximate all continuous functions from $\mathbb{R}^n$ to $\mathbb{R}^m$ in the topology of uniform convergence on compact subsets. We show that whenever the real projective space $\mathbb{RP}^{n-1}$ admits a smooth immersion into $\mathbb{R}^n$, the minimal width is at least $n+\min\{n,m\}$, assuming that the activation function is continuous and monotone. As a consequence, the minimal width of ReLU networks is $n+m$ whenever $n$ is equal to 2, 3, 4, 7 or 8 and $1\le m \le n$, extending results of Hanin-Sellke and Hwang.
item.dc:creator: BaoZhi Chu, Ben Weinkove

item.title: Backtracking Direct, Indirect and Total Effects
item.description: arXiv:2610.28910v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Natural direct and indirect effects are defined through cross-world interventional counterfactuals. We propose an alternative construction based on backtracking counterfactuals. Rather than intervening on the treatment or mediator and change the structural equations, we use a backtracking conditional distribution to construct an alternative exogenous state satisfying a desired treatment-mediator constraint and then evaluate the unchanged structural equations on that state. This yields the backtracking direct and indirect effects, and also the backtracking total effect. Likewise, we adapt the population intervention effects.
item.dc:creator: Jose M. Pe\~{n}a

item.title: Unintended Side Effects of Value Training in LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2610.29922v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: As LLMs are increasingly deployed in value-sensitive contexts, aligning them with human values has emerged as a post-training objective in NLP, aimed at instilling additional values and guiding model behaviour. However, current evaluations remain narrow. Because values are interconnected, it is unclear how fine-tuning for specific values alters unrelated capabilities and behaviours. In this work, we adapt four instruction-tuned LLMs across individual Hofstede's value dimensions and evaluate them on both cross-value transfer and broader behaviours. We find that value-specific training produces unintended side effects on untrained values, risk preferences, social cognition, and safety traits. Consequently, we suggest that value alignment after post-training should incorporate broader behavioral evaluations, and we highlight the need to investigate where additional value training might best fit into the pipeline. We release all 48 value-tuned model checkpoints at https://huggingface.co/sidicity/cultural-value-models
item.dc:creator: Siddhesh Pawar, Chen Cecilia Liu, Anna Korhonen, Isabelle Augenstein

item.title: Measure Before You Train: Typed Decision Models vs. a Classical Baseline vs. a Generative LLM for Routing a Personal Multilingual Inbox
item.description: arXiv:2610.32955v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Personal email agents decide, for every message, its type and urgency and whether to draft a reply, create a task or ignore it. In production these decisions are delegated to a generative LLM or to rules, and their error rate is rarely measured: the stored labels were written by the system itself. We describe Foyer, a self-hosted personal inbox agent, and a measurement protocol (stratified sampling, frozen snapshots, thread-grouped splits, secret redaction, human labels in the review loop) that produces ground truth before any training. On 231 emails in Italian and English we compare eleven systems: the stored production type, a TF-IDF + logistic-regression baseline, local and hosted typed decision models (Tev1, Nimble, Jeva, Jev) and generative LLMs. Four results. The stored production type scores 28% against a 57% majority class. With about two hundred labels a logistic regression has the highest point accuracy on every field (type 0.77 +/- 0.02 over five seeds) at a thousandth of the latency, but on every field at least one hosted model is statistically indistinguishable from it (exact McNemar, Holm-corrected). A generative model recovers part of the sender's relationship to the owner from the text (0.60); inheritance from the contact is right 98.6% of the time where the sender was seen before: it belongs in the contact graph, not in the prompt. Per-email accuracy is not the product metric: composed into actions, the classifier ignores 18% of the emails that needed action, against 4% for the best generative model; a cost-chosen threshold cuts that to 10%, indistinguishable from the hosted decision model's; on the adversarial corpus the thresholded classifier is the cheapest system above a missed-email price of 4. Two blind annotators agree with the reference at kappa 0.81 and 0.86 on type. v4 corrects threshold results computed on a truncated corpus in v1-v3.
item.dc:creator: Federico Lucca

item.title: Controlled Block Proximal Linearized Method for Nonconvex and Nonsmooth Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2610.34390v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this paper, we consider multiblock nonconvex and nonsmooth optimization without assuming bounded iterates or coercivity of the original objective. We propose the Controlled Block Proximal Linearized (CBPL) method, whose control potentials establish boundedness while retaining the original objective, constraints and variables. We prove finite length and whole-sequence convergence to an effective critical point of the original objective, where one limiting subgradient annihilates all effective feasible directions. We establish finite total variation of the original objective and block functions, summable original effective residuals, and finite termination and linear or sublinear convergence rates for the original objective values. Scale orthogonality further gives full original criticality and, for homogeneous balancing controls, summable absolute objective errors with an $o(1/K)$ best-iterate bound. We establish a complete degeneracy theory for graph-regularized nonnegative factorizations: scale criticality is equivalent to graph collapse, and full criticality eliminates graph action; our controls prevent this collapse while retaining genuine reconstruction changes. Furthermore, our proposed method provides the practical, simple, and effective schemes for these applications, combining guaranteed convergence with explicit closed-form updates that can be applied directly to solve the original problems. We apply CBPL to graph-regularized sparse nonnegative matrix factorization with $\ell_0$-constraints ($\ell_0$-GSNMF), graph-regularized sparse nonnegative canonical polyadic (CP) decomposition with $\ell_0$-constraints ($\ell_0$-GSNCP), and graph-regularized sparse nonnegative independent-core matrix tri-factorization with $\ell_0$-constraints ($\ell_0$-GSNMTF). Numerical experiments demonstrate effectiveness, convergence and structural control.
item.dc:creator: Weifeng Yang

item.title: Model Selection for Off-Policy Evaluation via Bellman Tournaments
item.description: arXiv:2610.35748v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Model selection and hyperparameter tuning pose a central challenge in off-policy evaluation (OPE) because estimation errors in fitted $Q$-functions and occupancy ratios cannot be directly evaluated using held-out transition data. Existing Bellman-residual-based validation methods often require auxiliary regressions, while many minimax-based methods require optimization over separate critic classes. We propose pairwise Bellman validation (PBV), a family of penalized Bellman tournament methods that reduces validation to computing held-out sample averages. PBV constructs critics from pairwise candidate differences, on the log scale for occupancy ratios, and selects the candidate with the smallest worst-case penalized score. This construction approximates oracle critics given by $Q$-function errors and log ratios of candidate to true occupancy ratios, whose Bellman and adjoint Bellman moments control estimation error. Critic penalties account for approximation error under candidate-class misspecification. We establish finite-sample oracle inequalities relative to the best available candidate, even under candidate-class misspecification. For $Q$-function selection, unweighted PBV avoids importance weighting but requires a coercivity condition on a quadratic form induced by the Bellman operator. Importance-weighted PBV (IW-PBV) uses marginalized importance weighting to exploit Bellman contraction under the target-policy occupancy measure, avoiding this condition. For occupancy-ratio selection, adjoint PBV (A-PBV) exploits KL contraction of the adjoint Bellman operator to obtain oracle guarantees under the offline data law. On Hopper and DeepOPE, unweighted PBV is competitive with LSTD-Tournament, often achieving higher accuracy on Hopper, while importance weighting can further improve performance under controlled overlap.
item.dc:creator: Lars van der Laan, Vasilis Syrgkanis, Nathan Kallus

item.title: Geometry Matters in Packed 3D Attention
item.description: arXiv:2610.38694v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Packing a 3D field into a token sequence gives every token two indices: a coordinate in the sample and a position in memory. Raster, Morton, and block-contiguous layouts change the position and leave the coordinate alone. A positional mechanism indexed by sequence position can therefore learn the memory layout rather than the object, and accuracy on the training layout cannot reveal that it has. We introduce PACK3D, a local-global attention operator that separates memory layout from attention geometry. It attends exactly within a coordinate-defined neighborhood, sees the whole field through pooled summaries, and rotates queries and keys with axial RoPE at token-grid coordinates. Because keys are rotated before pooling, each query-to-summary logit is a weighted sum of query-key terms evaluated at the summarized tokens' displacements from the query. The operator is equivariant to any repacking that carries coordinates, neighborhoods, summary memberships, and within-block slots along with the tokens. When evaluated on Allen WTC-11 microscopy at 262k tokens, PACK3D and a matched packed-sequence RoPE control reach comparable Dice on the training layout. Repacking the same validation volumes then costs the packed control 0.048 macro Dice on average, with a loss in all six seeds, while PACK3D changes by 0.0001. On MSD Heart and Spleen, sequence indexing again changes more predictions under repacking, at little cost in Dice. PACK3D also exceeds a parameter-matched 3D U-Net by 0.009 Dice over six seeds, and a full PACK3D layer runs within 7-31% of window-attention latency while adding a global pathway. Geometry, not storage order, should index attention over packed 3D fields. Code is available at https://github.com/amilworks/Pack3D.
item.dc:creator: Amil Khan, Anantajit Subrahmanya, B. S. Manjunath

item.title: Conditional Neural SDEs for Financial Time-Series Generation
item.description: arXiv:2610.41405v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Conditional generation of time-series paths is a central problem in probabilistic modeling, where the goal is to simulate future trajectories that are both realistic and responsive to external context. It has direct applications in finance and economics. Neural stochastic differential equations provide a natural framework for this task by combining continuous-time stochastic dynamics with learnable drift and diffusion functions. However, directly modeling the target state can be unstable in conditional settings, especially when the target and conditioning variables have strong level dependence, limited training data, or different dimensions. We propose a residual-anchor Neural SDE architecture that decomposes the target into a learned conditional anchor and a stochastic residual. The anchor captures the context-dependent baseline, while the Neural SDE (Stochastic Differential Equation) models the residual dynamics around this baseline. This separation reduces the burden on the stochastic dynamics and generalizes spread-based representations to more general conditioning settings. We evaluate the approach on real-world financial time series, including conditional interest-rate scenarios and a comparison with a time-series foundation model. The results show that the proposed model can generate plausible conditional paths, maintain competitive point accuracy, and provide calibrated uncertainty estimates.
item.dc:creator: Sina Molavipour, Alireza M. Javid, Bj\"orn L\"ofdahl, Mikhail Nechaev

item.title: Recovering Missing Degrees of Freedom in Simulation-Trained Field-Level Generative Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.02627v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Simulation-trained generative models are emerging as a powerful framework for field-level inference in cosmology, particularly in strongly nonlinear regimes where analytical approaches become intractable. However, the finite size of training datasets often leads to variance shrinkage, indicating that part of the realization-level variability of the underlying physical process is not captured by the learned generative dynamics. In this paper, we interpret variance shrinkage as a diagnostic of missing effective degrees of freedom and introduce physics-informed latent modifications to the generative dynamics of a continuous normalizing flow. We show that these latent corrections recover a substantial fraction of the missing variability without requiring additional training simulations. Using weak-lensing field-level inference as a representative cosmological application, we further demonstrate through posterior analysis that the learned latent directions are actively exploited during inference and behave as effective nuisance parameters that absorb part of the mismatch between the training and target distributions. As a result, the model exhibits improved robustness to out-of-distribution shifts in field-level inference. Our work establishes variance shrinkage as a practical diagnostic for identifying missing degrees of freedom in simulation-trained generative models and provides a framework for recovering them through physics-informed modifications of generative dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Masato Shirasaki, Shiro Ikeda

item.title: An Experimental Study of Hybrid Retrieval, NLI and Open-source LLMs for Scientific Claim Verification
item.description: arXiv:2611.03093v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Claim verification is the task of deciding whether a source text supports a claim, contradicts it, or lacks sufficient evidence. Natural Language Inference (NLI) models can judge whether a single sentence supports or contradicts a claim, but they struggle when the evidence is spread across several sentences. Conversely, Large Language Models (LLMs) can reason across sentences, but may draw conclusions the text does not support. In this experimental study, we test whether a conservative fusion rule, labeling a claim Support or Contradict only when both models agree and defaulting to Not Enough Evidence otherwise, combines their strengths. We construct a benchmark of 2,035 claims from SciFact and CliniFact (858 Support, 152 Contradict, 1,025 Not Enough Evidence). We retrieve the top five most relevant sentences per claim using a hybrid of semantic and lexical (BM25) retrieval, which slightly outperforms either method alone. These retrieved sentences are then provided to every verification model. We then compare a DeBERTa-v3-base-mnli-fever-anli NLI baseline against Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, and Mistral 7B. Qwen3 achieves the highest Macro-F1 (0.7937), followed by Llama 3.1 (0.7204) and Mistral (0.6388), while the NLI baseline reaches only 0.3157. Contrary to our hypothesis, fusion degrades performance, dropping Macro-F1 to 0.7392, 0.6730, and 0.5991, respectively. To understand this decline, we analyze agreements, disagreements, and common error patterns between the NLI and LLM verifiers. Our error analysis shows that NLI and LLM disagreements often result in correct LLM predictions being overturned.
item.dc:creator: Lakshmi Narayanan P, Narenkarthik K, Naren Kumar C

item.title: Reading Why: Born-Measured Attention with Exact Word Evidence on Light and Qubits
item.description: arXiv:2611.05355v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When a language model answers, we can usually only estimate why. We build a transformer in which every nonlinearity is a quadratic detection - an interference, a balanced reading or a camera - and the output is a Born probability: attention |<q|k>|^2, the form of the Born rule, normalised per row, a measured product for the feed-forward nonlinearity, and a Born readout; between detections, classical control rescales and re-encodes. With its denominators held at the input, each class probability is a polynomial in the word amplitudes, so its integrated-gradient evidence is computed by a finite quadrature with no quadrature error: the words' contributions sum to the class probability above its no-information share to 10^-13. On e-SNLI natural language inference it reaches 77.45 +- 0.91 % accuracy, level with a same-size softmax transformer (76.62 +- 0.36 %) and an order-free bag of embeddings (77.79 %). Exactness buys the sum, not the best ranking. Deleting the word its evidence ranks first changes the answer in 44 % of pairs, of the 53 % some deletion changes, against 31-32 % for the softmax model's integrated gradients; the model's own gradient x input does as well (43 %), as does a bag of embeddings' (43 %, seed 0), and leave-one-out does better. Holding the denominators helps the low end: the five words ranked last change the answer in 1 %, against 6 % free. The same weights compile exactly to simulated optoelectronics, and their attention to qubits. On ibm_kingston, reading only the attention, the device gave the model's answers in all three Hadamard-test runs (the two shortest pairs and one without its deciding word) and both compute-uncompute runs (one circuit per overlap); uniform attention answers otherwise on two of the three inputs. With the device's row sums the evidence correlated with the exact one at 0.997 and 0.962 by Hadamard tests; with compute-uncompute, 0.971 and 0.48.
item.dc:creator: Teerawat Tongloy, Jiraporn Pongsopa, Rangsan Jomtarak

item.title: NaijaFacts: A Framework for Disentangling Language from Knowledge in Facts about Nigeria
item.description: arXiv:2611.06504v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multilingual benchmarks for African languages mostly translate generic questions into local languages, measuring linguistic competence but not whether models know facts about Africa. We introduce NaijaFacts, a benchmark of factual and statistical questions about Nigeria, authored by native speakers and grounded in authoritative official statistics, with every question available in English, Nigerian Pidgin, Yor\`ub\'a, Igbo, and Hausa. Answering similar questions for the UK and US yields a country by language matrix that disentangles a language effect (the model knows the fact but degrades in a low-resource language) from a knowledge effect (the fact is absent in every language). Across eight frontier and Nigeria-adapted models, the knowledge effect dominates: English-query accuracy is 49-50% for the US/UK but 20% for Nigeria. The language effect is smaller and tracks web representation, degrading from English to Yor\`ub\'a (9 points on Nigeria, up to 24 on US/UK questions). We find scale does not help: the strongest models reach 66-79% on the UK and the US but none exceed 31% on Nigerian statistics. Extending to all 54 African countries with our best performing frontier model shows the same profile continent-wide, 96% on culture and 98% on politics against 26% on statistics, so the gap is not specific to Nigeria.
item.dc:creator: Zainab Afolabi, Nikita Kozodoi, Jack Butler, Babs Khalidson, Sabastine Dekaa Francis, Christiana I. Ezeilo, Olosunde Akinlolu Adesey

item.title: Label-Wording Augmentation in a Typed-Decision Encoder: Gains on Unfamiliar Words, Not on Abbreviations or Codes
item.description: arXiv:2611.08439v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Typed-decision models score options that the caller supplies at request time, so their accuracy depends on label wording that the model's developer does not control. We compare two releases of a 307M-parameter multilingual cross-encoder, Ru-Jev, trained on thirteen Russian-language tasks; the later release adds an augmentation that presents labels in several surface forms. Holding questions fixed and varying only how eighteen routing labels are worded, we evaluate ten label vocabularies at five and eighteen candidates, checked for overlap with the training data.
